segments.say: Why do so many people start new habits on New Year's Day? Or on a Monday? Or on the first day of the month, or after a birthday? There's nothing magical about these dates. Monday is just another day. And yet, they feel like natural starting points. Like turning a page.

In two thousand and fourteen, the researchers Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman and Jason Riis studied this pattern. They looked at several kinds of data. How often people searched for the word diet on Google. How often students went to a university gym. And when people signed up to commit to personal goals on a website.

show.who: Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman & Jason Riis
show.what: Researchers looked at Google searches for the word "diet", gym attendance, and sign-ups for goal-setting commitments around dates like new weeks, months, years and birthdays.

segments.say: And they found a clear pattern. Searches for diet, gym visits and goal commitments tended to rise at the start of new time periods. The beginning of a new week, a new month, a new year. After birthdays and holidays. The researchers called these moments temporal landmarks, and the pattern the fresh start effect.

Why would a date on the calendar matter? The researchers suggested that temporal landmarks help us separate our past selves from our present selves. The person who procrastinated last month belongs to the old chapter. The person starting today is new. That psychological distance from past failures can make it easier to begin again.

show.cap: A new page, a new beginning

segments.say: Landmarks may also encourage us to step back and think about the big picture. On a Monday morning or a birthday, we naturally reflect on where we are and where we want to go. That reflection can bring our goals back into focus, after weeks of being buried under daily busyness.

The lovely thing about this research is that you don't have to wait for New Year's Day. You can create your own fresh starts. The first day of spring. The day after a holiday. The start of a new project. Even tomorrow morning, if you decide it marks a new beginning. The landmark is partly in how we frame it.

There's a small trap here, though. Waiting for a fresh start can itself become a form of procrastination. I'll start my new routine next Monday. And then next Monday comes, and it's next month instead. So it can help to use fresh starts as a boost, not as an excuse to delay. If a landmark is close, use it. If not, the next hour can be a fresh start too.

Fresh starts are also helpful after slips. If you've been procrastinating for a week, it's easy to feel that the week is ruined, so why bother. That's sometimes called the what the hell effect. But you can treat tomorrow, or even this afternoon, as a fresh start. One bad week doesn't have to become a bad month.

There's a gentle wisdom in this. Every morning is, in a sense, a small fresh start. You wake up, and the day is new. Whatever happened yesterday, you can begin again. You don't need to carry the weight of every past delay. You can set it down, and take one small step today.

show.cap: Every day is a new day.

segments.say: Seen this way, a fresh start isn't about pretending the past didn't happen. It's about giving yourself permission to move forward without dragging guilt behind you. And as we'll see in the next part, letting go of guilt may be one of the most effective things a procrastinator can do.

So here's what the fresh start effect teaches us. New weeks, months and years tend to spark goal pursuit. Temporal landmarks help us separate our old self from our new self. You can create your own fresh starts. And it's wise not to let waiting for a fresh start become another way of putting things off.

show.title: Fresh starts
items: New weeks, months and years spark action
Landmarks separate old self from new
You can create your own fresh starts

segments.say: Now we come to one of the most surprising findings in all of procrastination research. Many people believe that feeling guilty about procrastinating will motivate them to do better next time. But a study of university students found that the opposite may be true.
